ops.rationale: Scopes the abstract's gap to the comparison across representation families with hand-crafted features among them, names the clusterer of 0.885, 0.711 and the federated values, and gives the extraction cost its own sentence.

States of the closest benchmark only what it says (foundation models compared with one another, separability pooled over 12-lead datasets with PTB-XL among them, no hand-crafted features, no MIT-BIH), and cites the image-model result for the separability-clusterability gap while the dominant-axes sentence stays the authors' own.
ops.new_text:
A representation can carry information about a label and still fail to cluster by it.
Linear separability and clusterability are distinct properties: a representation may
place the discriminative direction far from its dominant axes of variation, so that a
supervised probe recovers the label while an unsupervised partition does not. \rev{In self-supervised image models, two layers with nearly the same linear-probe accuracy can differ notably in clustering quality \cite{sslclustering2025}, and we treat this distinction as background rather than as a finding.} What
has not been measured, for ECG, is how the common representation families compare on
this axis under proper chance-corrected metrics.
\rev{The most directly related work benchmarks several ECG foundation models against one another and includes a cluster-separability analysis pooled over 12-lead datasets, PTB-XL among them \cite{lookingbeyond2026}. It adds no hand-crafted features, and its datasets do not include the MIT-BIH database.} \rev{A comparison with hand-crafted features matters because they are interpretable and need no training, and MIT-BIH adds a beat-morphology task to the rhythm task of PTB-XL.}

ops.rationale: Gives the patient-grouped rule and the supervised ceiling in the first contribution in a form of its own, so that it no longer copies the abstract's definitions word for word.

Says the contrastive methods preceded the foundation models and describes CLOCS, 3KG and contrastive predictive coding each by what its source holds, names the four families of the study with the foundation models placed among them, and gives the tensor arm its own sentence.
ops.new_text:
\paragraph{Unsupervised ECG and representations.} Hand-crafted features built from
RR-interval irregularity and beat morphology encode the defining signatures of common
arrhythmias and underpin decades of automatic analysis \cite{hrvstandards1996,dechazal2004}.
Tensor and wavelet decompositions have been combined with spectral clustering for
unsupervised 12-lead classification \cite{wavelettensorecg2018}. \rev{Reconstruction autoencoders are trained to reproduce the signal, an objective that rewards signal energy and does not ask the bottleneck to separate classes, so such a bottleneck may encode a class without arranging it into clusters.} \rev{Contrastive self-supervised methods for the ECG preceded the foundation models below. CLOCS \cite{clocs2021} builds on patient- and lead-level invariances, and 3KG \cite{threekg2021} on physiologically motivated augmentations. Contrastive predictive coding for 12-lead ECG adapts a self-supervised method from other domains \cite{mehari2022ssl}.} Self-supervised and foundation models for
ECG, such as HuBERT-ECG \cite{hubertecg2024} and ECGFounder \cite{ecgfounder2024}, learn
general representations from millions of recordings and are now evaluated as frozen
feature extractors. \rev{The wavelet-tensor and spectral-clustering method of \cite{wavelettensorecg2018} addresses a related unsupervised goal with a different (tensor) representation. This study compares four representation families: raw flattening, the conv-AE, hand-crafted features and frozen foundation-model embeddings. Raw flattening and the conv-AE encode signal energy, through the sample amplitudes and the reconstruction objective. The foundation-model embeddings place each record in a feature space fixed by large-scale pretraining, and the hand-crafted features encode the quantities that define the classes. A tensor arm is left to future work.}

ops.rationale: The source computes the ARI over 12-lead datasets pooled, PTB-XL one of them, and not on PTB-XL alone.
ops.new_text:
\paragraph{Closest benchmark.} \rev{The ECG foundation-model benchmark of \cite{lookingbeyond2026} reported the cluster-separability (ARI) of foundation-model embeddings pooled over 12-lead datasets, PTB-XL among them, and found that some models clustered by clinical label while others clustered by dataset. It compared foundation models to one another and stated that prior work omits a representation-wise evaluation. It did not add a hand-crafted baseline, and it did not include MIT-BIH.} We fill both gaps and add a supervised ceiling so that
a low clustering score can be attributed to geometry rather than to missing information.

ops.rationale: Attributes 21 799 records from 18 869 patients to version 1.0.3, the version the availability statement names, gives the descriptor's 21 837 and 18 885 as what the cited paper reports, and states the patient grouping as the cohort's procedure.
ops.new_text: \paragraph{PTB-XL.} \rev{We used PTB-XL, a public 12-lead database, in its version 1.0.3, which holds 21\,799 records from 18\,869 patients. The paper that describes the database \cite{ptbxl2020} reports 21\,837 records from 18\,885 patients. Each record holds one 10\,s signal of twelve leads, called a strip below. Rhythm labels were taken from the SCP-ECG (Standard Communications Protocol for Computer-Assisted Electrocardiography) statements. The SR-versus-AF cohort used as positives all records carrying an AF statement, AFIB (atrial fibrillation) or AFLT (atrial flutter), so atrial flutter records were counted as AF positives. Sinus-rhythm records without any AF statement served as controls.} PTB-XL encodes rhythm statements at a likelihood of zero meaning ``present'', \rev{so a presence-based rule was required, since a confidence threshold would discard every SR record. We drew a balanced, patient-disjoint cohort of 2\,542 records (1\,282 SR, 1\,260 AF), so the majority-class baseline is 0.504. Records were taken from the \mbox{100\,Hz} release of the database as signals of 1000 samples by 12 leads. No filtering, resampling or rescaling was applied before each representation's own preprocessing, so every representation started from the same signal. The lead set was chosen per representation and is stated with each representation below. Every fold of the evaluation was drawn by patient, and no patient contributed records to both classes.}

ops.rationale: Cites the database for itself and PhysioNet for the route by which it is distributed.
ops.new_text: \paragraph{MIT-BIH.} \rev{For generalization we used the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database \cite{mitbih2001}, distributed through PhysioNet \cite{physionet2000}. Each annotated beat was segmented into a window of $[-300, +250]$\,ms around the R-peak across both leads. We formed a balanced normal-versus-premature-ventricular (N-vs-V) task of 3\,000 beats (1\,500 per class) from 47 records, with the record as the grouping unit, so that the beats of one record never fell in two folds. This is a morphology task and a deliberate contrast to the PTB-XL rhythm task. In PTB-XL the two classes differ in the rhythm of a 10\,s strip, whereas in MIT-BIH they differ in the shape of a single beat. The second task therefore tests whether the ordering of the representations depends on the kind of class difference.}

ops.rationale: Drops the claim that a single-lead definition is what suited the two-lead beats, words the Challenge citation as its source states it, and scopes the lead set to the 12-lead versions used, with the reason for leaving the foundation models off MIT-BIH given here once.
The source defines FedAvg for locally trained models, so the federated k-means is described as weighted averaging of the site centroids by analogy with it, without calling it standard.
ops.new_text: \rev{To probe deployment under data siloing we used federated $k$-means, in which the server averages the site centroids with weights, as FedAvg averages locally trained models \cite{fedavg2017}. The 2\,542 records were partitioned, patient-grouped, across ten simulated sites, either independently and identically distributed (IID) or with class proportions drawn from a Dirichlet distribution so that sites differed sharply in arrhythmia prevalence (non-IID). The Dirichlet concentration was 0.3, applied per class over the ten sites, and any site left holding fewer records than clusters was dropped. Feature scaling was fitted once on the full representation matrix before partitioning, so the federation concerned the clustering step alone. Separate sites would not share these pooled statistics, a limitation taken up in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. Federated clustering consisted of fifteen aggregation rounds of three local Lloyd iterations per site. In each round the server replaced each centroid by the mean of the site centroids, weighted by the number of records each site assigned to it, and the centroids were initialised globally from two randomly drawn records. Both settings were repeated over ten seeds, with the site partition and the centroid initialisation redrawn at each seed. We report the global ARI relative to centralized clustering of the same representation.}

ops.rationale: The random forest shows only that a non-linear readout recovers what the linear probe missed, so the link to misalignment is stated as consistent with it and not as shown.
ops.new_text: \rev{The raw and conv-AE representations both sat at a majority-class assignment under all five clusterers, for different reasons. The conv-AE ceiling of 0.678 is what a bottleneck optimised to reconstruct signal energy retains of a class it was never asked about, and it recovered 0.008. Raw flattening reached a ceiling of 0.519 against a majority of 0.504, so a linear probe found almost no label in the 1992-dimensional vector. Its coordinates are amplitudes at fixed sample offsets, and a likely cause of this linear failure is that no fixed offset falls on the same part of the cardiac cycle in two records. A random forest on the same vector reached 0.714. A non-linear readout thus recovered label information that the linear probe missed, which is consistent with misalignment as the cause. The raw representation therefore lacks linearly recoverable label information, while the conv-AE holds label information without arranging it into clusters, and changing the clustering algorithm addresses neither.}

ops.rationale: States the off-axis reading as this study's own, tested out of fold, and cites the source only for a comparable gap in self-supervised image models.
ops.new_text: \rev{The supervised ceilings (last column of Table~\ref{tab:main} and Fig.~\ref{fig:sep}) exposed a gap between separability and clusterability. The raw representation carried almost no linearly recoverable label information (ceiling 0.519, barely above the 0.504 majority), consistent with its chance-level clustering. The conv-AE was more separable (0.678) yet still clustered at chance (best ARI 0.008, from Ward agglomerative clustering), so the conv-AE encoded the class without organising it into clusters. HuBERT-ECG was the sharpest case, with a ceiling of 0.899 but an ARI of only 0.195. ECGFounder and the hand-crafted features achieved both high separability and high clusterability. This study reads the gap of the weaker embeddings as one of geometry: their discriminative information exists but does not lie along their dominant axes of variation. A comparable gap between linear-probe accuracy and clustering quality has been reported for self-supervised image models \cite{sslclustering2025}.}

ops.rationale: Says the fraction 1.00 is rounded to two decimals and bounds the records outside the largest cluster at 12 of 2 542 from that rounding, and gives the paragraph the count of the silhouette panel so that its length follows its own content.
ops.new_text: \rev{Internal indices misled here in a specific, reproducible way. Raw flattening with agglomerative clustering attained a silhouette of 0.81 while the ARI was 0.000 and its largest cluster held a fraction of 1.00 of the cohort. That fraction is rounded to two decimals, so at most 12 of the 2\,542 records lay outside the largest cluster. The hand-crafted representation, which recovered the classes (ARI 0.711, balanced clusters), had a \emph{lower} silhouette of 0.28. Fig.~\ref{fig:trap} plots 157 clustering solutions, which cover 22 of the 25 representation-by-clusterer cells. The three cells left out are HDBSCAN fits that labelled the whole cohort as noise, for which the silhouette is undefined. Across the plotted solutions the degenerate one-cluster solutions attained a high silhouette at zero ARI. A degenerate one-cluster solution maximises compactness while carrying no class information. This is the artefact behind the original project's silhouette of 0.89, and it is why chance-corrected external metrics, read together with cluster-size sanity checks, are necessary.}

ops.rationale: Brings the MIT-BIH ceilings of the table caption into the text with what the raw-beat ceiling means, so that the paragraph's length follows its content.
ops.new_text: \rev{The ordering of the representations replicated on a different dataset and a different task type (Table~\ref{tab:mitbih}). On the N-vs-V beat-morphology task the 21-dimensional beat-morphology feature set clustered well (ARI 0.783), whereas the raw beat window did not (ARI 0.018 with $k$-means and 0.049 with agglomerative clustering), although the beats were R-peak aligned. The supervised ceiling of the raw beat window was 0.741 on this balanced task, against 0.925 for the beat-morphology features. A supervised probe thus found label information in the raw beat window that its clustering did not recover. The conv-AE was again the clean separability-versus-clusterability case, with a supervised ceiling of 0.927 but a best ARI of only 0.127, from the Gaussian mixture. The same pattern appeared for rhythm on PTB-XL and for morphology on MIT-BIH, which supports the representation-level reading of the PTB-XL results.}

ops.rationale: Scopes the caption's statement to the 12-lead versions used, since the published ECGFounder also has a single-lead model.
Gives the memory comparison and the absence of learned parameters each its own sentence.
ops.new_text: \rev{Table~\ref{tab:cost} gives the cost of computing each representation, which bears on deployment alongside the ARI. ECGFounder, which clustered best, was the most expensive per record, at fifteen times the hand-crafted extraction. Both foundation models needed a gigabyte or more of resident memory against \mbox{364\,MB} for the hand-crafted features, about a third of the memory of ECGFounder. The hand-crafted features also carry no learned parameters. Clustering itself was negligible everywhere, under \mbox{0.3\,s} for the whole cohort at any of the five dimensionalities, so the cost of a representation is the cost of extracting it.}

ops.rationale: Scopes both lead clauses of the decision rule to the versions tested and joins the cost paragraph to the rule it supports.
ops.new_text: \rev{The practical reading is a decision rule for the two tasks evaluated here: SR-versus-AF rhythm separation on PTB-XL and N-vs-V beat morphology on MIT-BIH. If the data are balanced and come in the 12-lead format that the tested version of ECGFounder takes, ECGFounder gives the best unsupervised separation here. The 16 hand-crafted features are the better choice if the data are imbalanced or siloed across sites, or if interpretability or low dimensionality matters. They are also the choice when the leads on hand are not the twelve that the tested foundation-model versions take. On the PTB-XL cohort they come within reach of ECGFounder on balanced data, overtake it under the 9:1 imbalance (ARI 0.265 against 0.063), and vary far less over the site draws of non-IID federation. The cost comparison of Table~\ref{tab:cost} supports the same rule. The representation that retains the most ARI under both stressors is also the less costly of the two to compute, and its 16 coordinates are clinical quantities that a reader can inspect for each record. Choosing the hand-crafted features for their behaviour under imbalance or federation therefore costs neither compute nor interpretability.}

ops.rationale: The cost paragraph now stands, word for word, at the end of the decision-rule paragraph (OP016).

Scopes the MIT-BIH statement to the foundation-model versions tested and drops single-lead as the reason the hand-crafted design carried over, since the lead set of the 21-dimensional features is not stated.
ops.new_text: \rev{The lead constraint is concrete. Neither foundation model version tested could embed the 2-lead MIT-BIH beats, whereas the hand-crafted design carried over to them through a separate beat-level feature set of the same kind. The raw and conv-AE representations, including the original project's design, are not viable for label-free arrhythmia structure on these tasks. On PTB-XL they were indistinguishable from predicting the majority class under all five clusterers. On MIT-BIH their best ARIs were 0.127 for the conv-AE and 0.049 for the raw beat window, against 0.783 for the beat-morphology features.}

ops.rationale: Describes the source as a benchmark of ECG foundation models that includes a cluster-separability analysis, and cites FedAvg for the weighted averaging the centroid aggregation follows.
Names ECG-FM as the model not included that the source reports to separate clinical labels, and moves here the missing MIT-BIH arm, which concerns the coverage of the foundation-model arm.
ops.new_text: \rev{We evaluated two foundation models. Others were not included, among them ECG-FM, whose embeddings the benchmark of \cite{lookingbeyond2026} reported to separate clinical labels. Neither of the two was evaluated on MIT-BIH, for the reason given in Section~\ref{sec:methods}. The MIT-BIH results thus compare the hand-crafted, conv-AE and raw representations only. The input of one of the two was also shorter than that of every other arm. HuBERT-ECG received the first \mbox{5\,s} of each \mbox{10\,s} strip and so saw fewer RR intervals, while every other arm saw the full strip. The shorter window is therefore an alternative explanation for its weak clustering, beside the off-axis geometry measured in Section~\ref{sec:results} and the organisation by dataset that \cite{lookingbeyond2026} reported for some foundation models.}

ops.rationale: Splits the paragraph by limitation: the binary tasks keep their paragraph, the flutter positives get one of their own, and the MIT-BIH sentence stands in the foundation-model paragraph (OP020).
ops.new_text:
\rev{Both evaluated tasks are binary by design, one rhythm contrast and one morphology contrast, each chosen so that the class definition is unambiguous and a clustering failure can be charged to the representation rather than to label noise. No multi-class arrhythmia cohort was evaluated, and no result here is a statement about multi-class arrhythmia structure, where several rhythms share an irregularity signature and the largest class outnumbers every minority. A multi-class PTB-XL rhythm cohort over the same embeddings is the least costly way to test whether the ordering survives that setting.}

\rev{The AF class of the rhythm task also counted atrial flutter records as positives. The cohort took every record with an AFIB or AFLT statement as AF (Section~\ref{sec:methods}). Flutter need not show the irregular rhythm on which the reading of Section~\ref{sec:intro} rests, so those records may sit closer to the SR class than the AF definition suggests. The ARI of every representation was computed against these labels, and no result here separates the flutter records from the fibrillation records. Removing the AFLT records, or giving them a class of their own, would show how far they move the ARI of each representation.}

\section*{Code and data availability}
PTB-XL (version 1.0.3) \cite{ptbxl2020} and the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (version 1.0.0) \cite{mitbih2001} are public
\rev{on PhysioNet \cite{physionet2000}.} The benchmark code, with the exact cohort
definitions, is available at \url{https://github.com/TheAxeC/ecg-representation-clustering}.
